newsitem.title: USA: Ohio to reject Columbia/HCA Blue Cross deal.
newsitem.headline: Ohio to reject Columbia/HCA Blue Cross deal.

text.p: The state of Ohio has said it plans to reject the proposed $299.5 million acquisition of most of Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Ohio by a for-profit hospital chain, Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp.

"The superintendent of insurance intends to disapprove the proposed transaction," the Ohio Department of Insurance said in a statement late Wednesday. Not-for-profit Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Ohio has 30 days to request a hearing on the decision.
Wall Street analysts said the rejection was irrelevant to investors in Nashville-based Columbia/HCA, the nation's largest provider of health care services.
Columbia/HCA has 343 hospitals and 147 surgery centers plus other types of facilities. In 1996 it earned $1.5 billion $2.22 a share on revenues of $19.9 billion.

"This is not an issue in any way, shape or form," Dean Witter Reynolds health care services analyst Todd Richter said. Wall Street had expected the merger was unlikely to come about, he said, adding it was a "tiny deal" for Columbia.
Kenneth Abramowitz, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Co., agreed. "It's been an interesting side show," he said.
Columbia was off 3/8 to 43-3/4 on the New York Exchange.
A Columbia spokeswoman said Thursday the company had just received the state's documents so was not prepared to comment.
"We are in the process of ... studying the implications," spokeswoman Eve Hutcherson told Reuters in a telephone interview. "The next steps are not clear to us at this point."
The state said the deal was not in the public interest and could adversely affect policy holder interests.
It questioned the valuation of the deal and payments that would be made to some Blue Cross executives and board members and said Blue Cross did not adequately solicit other suitors.
A Blue Cross of Ohio spokeswoman said the insurer plans to issue a statement but she could not comment immediately.

The ruling comes amid turmoil in Blue Cross's executive offices after the insurer said it lost $95 million in 1996. Earlier this week, chief executive officer John Burry sought to fire president Kent Clapp. Then the insurer's board, including Clapp, voted to oust Burry. Spokeswoman Suzanne Martin said it remained unclear who will end up at the helm.

The Columbia deal had been under fire from various fronts, including the Chicago-based national Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association, Ohio's attorney general and various groups representing some policy holders, consumers and trade unions.
